title: Mobile Security: the APK under the microscope
description: Android app anatomy, static analysis with apktool/jadx, TLS pinning and Frida: how a mobile app is audited.

1.title: APK anatomy and static analysis
1.body:
## Inside the APK

```bash
unzip -l target.apk
# classes.dex      ← the code (Dalvik/ART bytecode)
# AndroidManifest.xml (binary)
# res/, assets/, lib/ (native .so), META-INF/ (signatures)
```

## The static duo: apktool + jadx

```bash
# apktool: readable resources + manifest + smali
apktool d target.apk -o target-unpacked
cat target-unpacked/AndroidManifest.xml | head -40

# jadx: logic in readable Java
jadx target.apk -d target-jadx
grep -rn "http://" target-jadx/sources/ | head    # plain HTTP?
grep -rni "api_key\|secret\|token" target-jadx/sources/ | head
```

## The static manifest checklist

The first thing you read in any audit:

| Indicator | Risk |
|---|---|
| `android:exported="true"` without a permission | Another, malicious app can launch it |
| `android:allowBackup="true"` | The data leaks out via adb backup |
| `debuggable="true"` in release | Attachable debugging = readable memory |
| `READ_SMS`/`ACCESSIBILITY` permissions with no justification | Overpermission |
| `usesCleartextTraffic="true"` | Plain HTTP allowed |

Then comes the code: hardcoded credentials (strings and grep), internal
API URLs (which reveal infrastructure), debugging flags, and
storage (`getSharedPreferences`/SQLite in cleartext vs
EncryptedSharedPreferences).

## OWASP MASVS and MASTG

The mobile reference framework (the equivalent of the web ASVS): **MASVS**
defines the requirements (storage, crypto, authentication, network,
resilience...) and **MASTG** the testing methodology, with recipes per
platform. The findings above map directly to MASVS-STORAGE and
MASVS-NETWORK.

The next task breaks through the most common barrier when static analysis is not
enough: the app you can only understand by watching it run — and that protects its
traffic with TLS pinning.

mobile-security-t01-q01.prompt: Structurally, what is an APK file?
mobile-security-t01-q01.hint: Look at the first command in the theory: if unzip -l can list its contents, you already know what kind of container it is.

options.a: A native ELF executable compiled for ARM that Android launches directly
options.b: A ZIP with classes.dex (Dalvik bytecode), compiled resources, a binary manifest and a signature
options.c: An encrypted disk image that only Google Play can decrypt
options.d: A single JAR with standard Java bytecode for the desktop JVM

mobile-security-t01-q02.prompt: Which tool decodes the binary AndroidManifest.xml and the resources into readable form (smali/xml)?
mobile-security-t01-q02.hint: apktool d app.apk — the standard for resources and smali

mobile-security-t01-q03.prompt: Which tool decompiles DEX bytecode to readable JAVA?
mobile-security-t01-q03.hint: jadx-gui (or the jadx CLI) — to read the logic without smali

mobile-security-t01-q04.prompt: In the manifest, which flag marks a component (Activity/Receiver/Service) as accessible by ANY app on the device?
mobile-security-t01-q04.hint: android:exported="true" — exported without a permission = inter-app attack surface

mobile-security-t01-q05.prompt: Which command (or grep over the decompiled output) hunts hardcoded URLs and API keys after unpacking?
mobile-security-t01-q05.hint: grep -r "http\|api[_-]\?key\|secret" over the apktool/jadx output folder

2.title: Dynamic analysis: Frida and TLS pinning
2.body:
## Watching the app run

The typical mobile lab: an emulator or rooted device + a proxy
(Burp/ZAP) + Frida server running on the Android device:

```bash
# On the device (root/emulator):
adb push frida-server /data/local/tmp/ && adb shell "/data/local/tmp/frida-server &"

# From your machine:
frida-ps -U                      # list the device's processes
objection -g com.target.app explore
# objection: a ready-made console with pinning bypass, class dumping, etc.
```

## The wall: TLS pinning

You set Burp as the system proxy, open the app... and it dies with a
network error. The app **pins** the real server's certificate and
rejects your CA. The standard bypass:

```bash
# Option 1 — objection (Frida under the hood):
objection -g com.target.app explore
android sslpinning disable

# Option 2 — universal Frida script:
frida -U -f com.target.app -l frida-multiple-unpinning.js --no-pause
```

After the bypass, the app talks through Burp and the real map of the API appears:
endpoints, tokens, parameters. That is where testing the logic begins
(BOLA in mobile APIs, poorly validated tokens, secrets in responses).

## What you hook with Frida (beyond pinning)

```javascript
// Example: see every HTTP request the app makes:
Java.perform(() => {
  const URL = Java.use('java.net.URL');
  URL.$init.overload('java.lang.String').implementation = function (u) {
    console.log('[URL]', u);
    return this.$init(u);
  };
});
```

Cleartext crypto, local storage, root detection (which gets bypassed
the same way), deep links... Frida is the Swiss Army knife: if the app does it at
runtime, you can see it and tamper with it.

## Mobile dynamic checklist

| Test | Tool |
|---|---|
| HTTPS traffic | Burp/ZAP + pinning bypass |
| Local storage | `adb shell run-as com.target.app ls` (debuggable) / root fs |
| Sensitive logs | `adb logcat | grep -i token` |
| Deep links | `adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "app://x"` |
| Resilience (root/emulator) | Frida hooks on the checks |

With static + dynamic analysis you have the full cycle of a mobile pentest —
and the same method carries over to iOS with different tooling (objection works the same way).

mobile-security-t02-q01.prompt: Which of these sentences best describes what Frida is?
mobile-security-t02-q01.hint: Look at the Java.perform example in the theory: that code runs INSIDE the app while it is running.

options.a: A decompiler that turns DEX bytecode into readable Java code
options.b: An HTTP proxy to intercept and modify the app's traffic
options.c: A framework that injects JavaScript into processes (native or Java) to hook functions on the fly
options.d: An Android emulator to run apps without a physical device

mobile-security-t02-q02.prompt: What is TLS certificate pinning and why does it break Burp/ZAP out of the box?
mobile-security-t02-q02.hint: Think about what happens when Burp presents its own certificate, signed by its CA, instead of the real server's certificate.

options.a: The app encrypts its requests twice and Burp can only decrypt one of the layers
options.b: The server blocks the IPs of well-known proxies such as Burp or ZAP
options.c: The app only accepts plain HTTP, so an HTTPS proxy sees nothing
options.d: The app embeds the fingerprint of the server's legitimate certificate and rejects the proxy's CA

mobile-security-t02-q03.prompt: What is the universal Frida script that bypasses pinning in hundreds of Android apps without writing code?
mobile-security-t02-q03.hint: Frida code-share: 'Android SSL Pinning Bypass' (httptoolkit / frida-multiple-unpinning)

mobile-security-t02-q04.prompt: Which Android network configuration file can authorize user CAs (letting Burp intercept without a bypass) — and is also a finding when misconfigured?
mobile-security-t02-q04.hint: networkSecurityConfig (trust-anchors): if it includes user certs, Burp works directly — a typical finding
